source.title: On the Dynamics of Delayed Generalization in Linear Models
source.authors: Atreya Vedantam; Nataraj Das; Chandrashekar Lakshminarayanan

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test accuracy over training time and reports delayed test generalization in controlled experiments, using a different model and setup from the original double-descent work.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-accuracy trajectories over training time, so these are rows for V2. It does not sweep model size or training-sample size. Bias and distance-from-origin measurements are not rows because they are not test error or test accuracy.
record.test_reason: The paper studies delayed generalization (grokking-like) in a linear model with a learnable bias on separable, noiseless data, and cites double descent only once in related work. Its only non-monotone test-accuracy curves come from a deliberately shifted test distribution, Pconc, packed against the decision boundary. The rise, dip and recovery there is driven by the bias drifting toward a support-vector imbalance. It is not test error on the training distribution as a model passes an interpolation threshold. On the standard in-distribution test set, accuracy reaches 1 within about 10^2 epochs, and MNIST test accuracy stays near 1. There is no model-size sweep, sample-size sweep, label-noise sweep or complexity re-count. The Pconc result is a related but different construct (sensitivity under distribution shift), so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that delayed generalization needs no depth and appears in a linear model with a learnable bias under full-batch gradient descent on separable data. Learning passes through three phases: population dominated, unlearning and generalization. The bias converges to −log δ, set by the support-vector imbalance, and generalization time is at least exponential in |log δ|. The delay is large only when test points lie near the boundary. The same bias behaviour appears at the MNIST output neuron, while its standard test accuracy stays near 1. They state they do not observe grokking in its usual form.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains fixed linear and MNIST models with full-batch gradient descent and tracks accuracy over time; it does not sweep model size or sample size as in the double-descent claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The delay depends on test distribution (standard versus concentrated) and support-vector balance; population imbalance adds a transient effect.

fits_no_version.finding: In a noiseless separable linear model with bias, accuracy on a test distribution concentrated near the boundary (Pconc) rises, collapses toward 1/2, then recovers after 10^5 to 10^6 epochs. The size of the delay grows with support-vector imbalance. On the in-distribution test set, accuracy reaches 1 within about 10^2 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-monotone test accuracy over training time (delayed generalization) can arise without depth, interpolation-threshold effects or label noise. It comes from implicit-bias drift of a learnable bias, and appears only on test distributions near the boundary.

record.code_released: Supplementary material is identified as containing code and reproduction details; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The checklist says the empirical results do not define error bars; synthetic experiments are conducted in d=2 with fixed seeds. The MNIST test uses a standard test set, not the concentrated distribution where the pronounced delay is demonstrated.

untested.parts: No epoch-wise test-error curve on the training distribution in a setting near an interpolation threshold or with label noise.
No capacity sweep across the interpolation point.

record.verdict_notes: Double descent appears only as a citation (Nakkiran et al.; Davies et al.) in related work. R7 and R8 duplicate R6 and R3 (same seeded runs replotted in Figure 3). The reader's labels (supports and limits_scope for V2) are removed: the Pconc curves come from an engineered distribution shift, and the in-distribution runs are not settings where V2 predicts a peak. If curators prefer to treat any non-monotone test curve over epochs as bearing on V2, then R2 and R4 to R6 would be T3 'observed' under distribution shift only, and R1, R16 and R17 would be 'absent' in distribution. That reading is not adopted here.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error peak near an interpolation threshold.
Other architectures, datasets, and training procedures beyond the reported synthetic linear-model experiments and the two MNIST runs.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes or test-risk curve across an interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
No label-noise or regularization sweep, and no test of multiple peaks or optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of model complexity by effective parameters.

rows.subject: linear model with bias
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent with exponential loss; test accuracy tracked over epochs.
rows.value: Test accuracy reaches 1 within about 10^2 epochs.
rows.note: The text states when accuracy reaches 1, but does not explicitly describe whether the trajectory has the full fall-rise-fall shape.
rows.check: Standard-test trajectory of a noiseless separable linear model. V2 concerns epoch-wise double descent; nothing in this setting makes V2 predict a peak, so the row bears on no version.

rows.subject: linear model with bias
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent with exponential loss; test accuracy tracked over epochs.
rows.value: Accuracy rises in Phase 1, dips in Phase 2, and recovers after about 10^5 epochs.
rows.note: This is the reported fall-rise-fall pattern in test error, expressed as rise-dip-recovery in accuracy.
rows.check: Rise, dip, recovery on the shifted test set Pconc with no planted support vectors. This is delayed generalization under distribution shift, not epoch-wise double descent on the training distribution. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: linear model with bias
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch gradient descent with exponential loss; test accuracy tracked over epochs.
rows.value: The authors report no delay for S(350,350).
rows.note: The balanced support-vector condition is compared with imbalanced support-vector conditions.
rows.check: Balanced support vectors give no delay on Pconc. This is a control within the paper's bias mechanism, not a measure of V2.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Linear model with concentrated test distribution Pconc and no planted support vectors; imbalanced support-vector configurations in Figure 2
reader_labels.reason: The test-accuracy trajectory rises, dips, and recovers on Pconc, and the text reports a collapse to 1/2 followed by delayed recovery for imbalanced support vectors (R2, R4–R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Standard test distribution, balanced support vectors, and the two MNIST standard-test runs
reader_labels.reason: The reported delay depends on test distribution and support-vector imbalance; the standard-test case reaches 1 within about 10^2 epochs, the balanced-support-vector condition has no delay, and MNIST test accuracy stays near 1 (R1, R3, R16, R17).
